name: Bing Places
why: Bing's map listings feed Bing search, Microsoft Copilot and ChatGPT's local answers.
steps: Search for your business on Bing Maps (the Check button).
Go to bing.com/forbusiness and sign in with a Microsoft account.
Claim the listing if it exists; otherwise create it. You can also import your Google Business Profile.
Verify it, then match your name, phone, address, hours and website to Google.

name: Apple Maps (Apple Business)
why: iPhone users find businesses in Apple Maps and through Siri, and both read this listing.
steps: Search for your business on Apple Maps (the Check button).
Go to business.apple.com and sign in with an Apple Account.
Claim your location, or add it if it's missing, and verify it.
Add hours, phone, website and photos, matching Google.

name: Yelp
note: Free; Yelp sells ads, which you don't need.
why: Yelp ranks in Google for local searches, and Apple Maps and AI assistants use its reviews.
steps: Open biz.yelp.com/claim and search for your business.
Claim it if it's listed; otherwise add it.
Verify by phone or email, then add hours, photos and services. Ignore the ad offers: the free listing is enough.

name: Facebook Page
why: Customers check Facebook for reviews, photos and hours, and Bing and AI assistants read it.
steps: From your personal Facebook account, open Pages > Create new Page.
Use your exact business name and pick your category.
Add your phone, address or service area, hours and website, the same as on Google.

name: BBB (Better Business Bureau)
note: The profile is free; accreditation is a paid extra you don't need.
why: A BBB profile is a trusted page that ranks for your name and shows customers you're real.
steps: Open bbb.org/get-listed.
Search for your business; claim it if it's there, otherwise request a free profile.
Fill in your details, the same as on Google. Skip accreditation unless you want it.

name: Nextdoor
why: Neighbours recommend local businesses on Nextdoor, and those recommendations show on your page.
steps: Open business.nextdoor.com/local and choose Claim your free Business Page.
Search for your business, then claim it or create it.
Add your services and service area, and ask happy customers to recommend you there.

name: Yellow Pages
note: Free listing; expect sales calls for paid add-ons.
why: An old, trusted directory that still ranks for business names and feeds other directories.
steps: Open yellowpages.com/claim-your-listing and search for your business.
Claim it, or add it if missing, using the same name, phone and address as Google.
Decline paid add-ons; the free listing is what counts.

name: Manta
why: A small-business directory that ranks for business names.
steps: Open Manta's free business listing page.
Search for your business, then claim or add it with the same details as Google.

name: Hotfrog
why: A free directory that adds another consistent mention of your name, phone and address.
steps: Open Hotfrog's Add a business page and create an account.
Add your business with the same details as Google. The paid add-on isn't needed.

name: Foursquare
note: Listing is free; claiming may ask for a small fee.
why: Foursquare's place data feeds many apps and car navigation systems.
steps: Open app.foursquare.com/venue/claim and search for your business.
Claim it if it's free to do so; otherwise make sure the listing's details are right.

name: LinkedIn Company Page
why: A company page ties your business to the people behind it, which Google and AI assistants use to trust it.
steps: From your LinkedIn account, open linkedin.com/company/setup/new.
Add your business name, website, logo and a short description.

name: Alignable
why: A local business network where other owners recommend you.
steps: Sign up for free at Alignable and create your business profile.
Use the same name, phone and town as Google.

name: Angi
note: Free profile; leads and ads cost money and are optional.
why: Homeowners search Angi for contractors, and Angi pages rank in Google for trade-plus-town searches.
steps: Open signup.angi.com/pro and create a free profile.
Add your services, service area, photos and license if you have one.
Skip paid leads and ads unless you want them: the profile itself is free.

name: Thumbtack
note: Free to join; you only pay for leads you choose to take.
why: A free profile that ranks for '<service> near <town>' searches.
steps: Open thumbtack.com/pro and create your profile.
Add services, photos and your service area. You can leave lead spending off.

name: Houzz
note: Free basic plan; Houzz Pro is paid and optional.
why: Homeowners browse Houzz for remodelers and installers, and project photos there rank in Google Images.
steps: Open pro.houzz.com/pro and choose the free basic plan.
Add your business details, service area and project photos.

name: Porch
note: Profile comes with joining; leads are paid.
why: Another home-services directory that ranks for trade searches.
steps: Open pro.porch.com/pro and create your profile.
Fill in services and service area. Buying leads is optional.

name: Bark
note: Free profile; answering leads costs credits.
why: A free service-business profile that ranks for service searches.
steps: Open Bark's sign-up page and create your free profile.
Add services and photos. You don't have to buy credits.

name: BuildZoom
why: BuildZoom lists licensed contractors from public license data and ranks for contractor names.
steps: Search for your business on buildzoom.com (it builds pages from public license records).
Open your page and press Claim now; it checks your license.
Add photos and services. Paid tiers are optional.

name: HomeGuide
note: Free profile; you pay only for leads you take.
why: A free home-services profile that ranks for '<service> cost <town>' searches.
steps: Open homeguide.com/pro and create your free profile.
Add services, photos and service area.
